questions.question: According to ⟨1117⟩, when should the pH of each batch of medium be confirmed, and within what range?

options.A: After cooling to room temperature (20°-25°C), within ±0.2 of the manufacturer's labeled value
options.B: Before sterilization while heated and dissolved, within ±0.5 of the manufacturer's labeled value, with no need to confirm again after sterilization
options.C: Only once for the first batch of each quarter, with the range set by the laboratory supervisor based on experience and no comparison to the labeled value
options.D: Only just before use in a 45°-50°C water bath, within ±1.0 of the labeled value, with no documentation needed

questions.explanation: The text requires the pH of each batch of medium to be confirmed after cooling to room temperature (20°-25°C), within ±0.2 of the manufacturer's labeled value, unless a validated method accepts a wider range. Unless otherwise specified, pH is not confirmed while hot or before sterilization, and there is no practice of "no need to document".
questions.reference: USP ⟨1117⟩ Media Preparation and Quality Control › Media Preparation

questions.question: A large volume of medium fills an autoclave, and the manufacturer recommends "121° for 15 minutes". What does this condition mean in ⟨1117⟩?

options.A: The autoclave set time, with 15 minutes counted from the start of heating regardless of the actual medium temperature, and no validation needed
options.B: It applies only to Purified Water; other liquid media must use dry heat sterilization at a higher temperature
options.C: The time the medium itself is at that temperature, to be applied in a validated autoclave according to validated parameters
options.D: Cooling the medium to 121° and then holding it for 15 minutes to ensure pH stability and avoid precipitation of medium components

questions.explanation: The text identifies 121° for 15 minutes as a common recommended sterilization cycle and stresses that these conditions refer to the time after the medium reaches that temperature, in a validated autoclave, with parameters set according to the manufacturer's or user's validation. Moist heat sterilization is the preferred method.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1117⟩ Media Preparation and Quality Control › Media Preparation

questions.question: Which practice for remelting solid media and holding molten agar is consistent with ⟨1117⟩?

options.A: The same bottle of medium may be melted repeatedly, as long as the pH is re-measured after each melting and recorded in the batch record
options.B: Solid medium in its original container without heat-labile components may be remelted only once; molten agar is held in a 45°-50°C water bath for no more than 8 hours
options.C: Molten agar should be held in a water bath above 60°C, and as long as the bath water is changed daily there is no limit on use period and no need to monitor bath temperature or holding time
options.D: Agar-containing plates should be stored in a -20°C freezer to extend shelf life and brought to room temperature before use

questions.explanation: The text recommends remelting only once, to avoid overheating or contamination affecting quality; molten agar should be kept in a monitored water bath set at 45°-50°C and not held longer than 8 hours (or as otherwise determined by the medium composition). Agar-containing plates must not be stored at 0° or below, to avoid destroying the gel structure.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1117⟩ Media Preparation and Quality Control › Media Storage

questions.question: A batch of medium fails growth-promotion testing, but a test using that batch has already been run and microorganisms grew. According to ⟨1117⟩, how should this be handled?

options.A: The batch can still be used, as long as a pH test is repeated and the result falls within the manufacturer's labeled range
options.B: The batch can be downgraded to non-critical testing with no investigation, simply by noting the downgraded use in the record and stopping use once the next batch arrives
options.C: The batch can still be used if the growth-promotion result differs from the previous batch by no more than one log, and no investigation is needed
options.D: The batch is not suitable for use and an investigation should be started; a failed growth-promotion result must not be used to invalidate a positive result

questions.explanation: The text states that medium that fails growth promotion is unsuitable for use and the cause should be investigated, and that a failed growth-promotion result cannot be used to invalidate a positive test result. Routine QC testing includes pH, growth promotion, inhibition and indicative properties.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1117⟩ Media Preparation and Quality Control › Quality Control Testing

questions.question: For media used for environmental monitoring in critical areas, what does ⟨1117⟩ prefer regarding packaging and sterilization?

options.A: Single-layer packaging is sufficient, with the outer layer wiped with alcohol before taking it directly into the critical area for use, and no preincubation
options.B: As long as the supplier has a shipment test report, no additional treatment or check is needed before taking it directly into the critical area
options.C: Preferably double-wrapped and terminally sterilized; if not terminally sterilized, 100% preincubated and inspected before entering the critical area
options.D: Always prepared on site in the critical area and used directly, to avoid contamination during transport, with no separate confirmation of sterility

questions.explanation: The text states that media used for environmental monitoring in critical areas are preferably double-wrapped and terminally sterilized; if not terminally sterilized, they should be 100% preincubated and inspected before use in the critical area. Media for sterility testing and environmental monitoring need special care.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1117⟩ Media Preparation and Quality Control › Quality Control Testing

questions.question: According to the seed-lot technique in ⟨1117⟩, which storage method allows cultures to be kept indefinitely?

options.A: On refrigerated agar slants at 2°-8°C, with colony appearance checked every quarter
options.B: At -70°C or lower, or in freeze-dried form
options.C: At -30°C, refrozen after each use and returned to the same freezer
options.D: In storage medium at room temperature, subcultured monthly, with the number of passages recorded after each subculture

questions.explanation: The text explains that the master stock is aliquoted and stored frozen at -30°C or lower until use; if stored at -70°C or lower, or in freeze-dried form, the culture can be kept indefinitely. Opened cell suspensions must not be refrozen.

questions.question: A laboratory prepared a working suspension from a frozen culture vial and some is left over. According to ⟨1117⟩, how should the remainder be handled?

options.A: Discard it and do not refreeze, to reduce the risk of loss of viability and contamination of the master stock
options.B: Refreeze it and keep it for the next use, which reduces waste, provided it is used up within three months
options.C: Return it to 2°-8°C and use it directly as a new master stock next time, noting the opening date on the label
options.D: Combine it with the next vial of culture to increase the cell count and use them together as the next working suspension

questions.explanation: The text states that after a culture vial is opened and a working suspension grown, the remaining cell suspension should not be refrozen and the unused portion should be discarded, to reduce the risk of loss of viability and contamination of the master stock. The number of passages of working cultures should also be tracked to avoid phenotypic changes from excessive subculturing.

questions.question: A laboratory is preparing to obtain cultures for compendial testing. According to ⟨1117⟩, which statement is correct?

options.A: Cultures can be bought from any commercial supplier without documentation, and used without confirmation as long as the label has the name and date and a supplier delivery note is attached
options.B: As long as the colony morphology matches, purity and identity need not be confirmed before use, and the culture can be used directly for compendial testing
options.C: Identity needs to be confirmed only to the family level, with no further identification to genus and species and no records kept
options.D: Cultures should come from a national culture collection or a qualified secondary supplier, with documentation of equivalence to the ATCC strain, and purity and identity should be confirmed before use

questions.explanation: The text requires cultures used for compendial testing to be obtained from a national culture collection or a qualified secondary supplier, with documentation of equivalence to the relevant ATCC strain; purity and identity must be confirmed before use in QC testing, and commonly used laboratory strains should ideally be confirmed to genus and species level.

questions.question: Which statement better reflects the ⟨1117⟩ principle on segregating laboratory equipment?

options.A: All equipment, whatever its type, must be separated into sterile-only and live-culture-only use with no sharing at all, even autoclaves being dedicated separately
options.B: Equipment that is difficult to disinfect, such as incubators and refrigerators, should be segregated from sterile operations and live culture work; the number of autoclaves is decided by resource considerations
options.C: Autoclaves must be divided into clean and waste types with no sharing, and the waste autoclave should be placed inside the aseptic area
options.D: Equipment that is difficult to disinfect needs no special segregation, as long as it is calibrated yearly and the exterior is wiped with disinfectant, with no distinction of use

questions.explanation: The text states that equipment that is difficult to disinfect (such as refrigerators and incubators) should be segregated from sterile operations (such as storing test media and incubating sterility test samples) and from live culture work. With proper maintenance, the contents of an autoclave are sterile after the cycle, so the number of autoclaves is decided by resource considerations and not to separate sterile from live culture work.

questions.question: When a laboratory introduces a new microbiological technology, what does ⟨1117⟩ require regarding personnel competence?

options.A: Only laboratory analysts need to be trained; supervisors and QA need no related skills and need not understand the principles and limitations of the new technology
options.B: Besides laboratory analysts, supervisors and QA who evaluate system suitability or deviations must also be able to analyze and interpret the complex data of the new technology
options.C: New technology is always interpreted by the equipment supplier, so the laboratory needs no written procedures and no ability of its own to interpret the data
options.D: Training is needed only once at acceptance, with no need afterwards to establish rules and principles or to periodically confirm that personnel competence is maintained

questions.explanation: The text states that introducing new technology requires new learning and training; besides laboratory analysts, supervisors and QA personnel who evaluate system suitability or deviations must be able to analyze and interpret the complex data generated by the new technology. Rules and principles should also be established for each new technology and included in written procedures to maintain consistency and accuracy.

questions.question: After colonies grow on environmental monitoring samples incubated in the clean area, where does ⟨1117⟩ say follow-up investigation work such as subculturing, staining or identification should be done?

options.A: Immediately in the clean area next to the original incubator, to avoid the contamination risk of moving the samples
options.B: Inside the sterility testing isolator, to ensure sterility of results and avoid cross-contamination
options.C: At any workbench with UDAF, with no need to consider the area or personnel flow
options.D: In the live culture section, with samples sent there promptly and without undue delay

questions.explanation: The text requires the laboratory to be divided into a clean or sterile area and a live culture area; once growth is detected, samples should be transferred from the clean area to the live culture area without unnecessary delay, where subculturing, staining, microbial identification and other investigational work is done. The area for handling and incubating environmental samples should be kept as free of live organisms as possible.

questions.question: In what environment does ⟨1117⟩ recommend sterility testing (of finished and in-process product, etc.) preferably be performed, and what can be used for less critical microbiological tests?

options.A: Sterility testing can be done on an ordinary laboratory bench; less critical tests must be done in an ISO 5 isolator
options.B: Sterility testing preferably in an ISO 5 isolator; less critical tests (such as bioburden) can use a UDAF workbench
options.C: Both sterility testing and bioburden testing should be done on an open bench in an ISO 8 cleanroom, with no isolator or UDAF
options.D: Sterility testing should be done at a UDAF workbench, with isolators used only for live culture work, and less critical tests must also use an isolator

questions.explanation: The text states that critical tests (such as sterility testing of finished product) should be performed under controlled conditions, with sterility testing preferably in an ISO 5 isolator. Less critical microbiological tests (such as bioburden samples of non-sterile products or intermediates) are suitably done at a unidirectional airflow (UDAF) workbench, whose air must meet the grade for which it was qualified.

questions.question: Water samples are sent to an external contract laboratory, and testing will not begin until 36 hours later. According to ⟨1117⟩, how should this be handled?

options.A: The sample can be frozen; extending the hold time does not affect viable counts, so even beyond 24 hours no additional supporting study is needed as long as the storage temperature is low enough
options.B: There is no problem; samples are acceptable under any conditions for up to 48 hours, regardless of storage temperature or sample type
options.C: Keep the sample at room temperature directly, since microorganisms do not change in storage, and test in order after the laboratory receives it
options.D: Acceptable storage is 2°-8°C for up to 24 hours; beyond that, it must be supported by an experimental study (such as a challenge test)

questions.explanation: The text explains that for monitoring water or bioburden before sterilization, samples may be held at 2°-8°C for up to 24 hours; if testing cannot be done within 24 hours (for example when using a contract laboratory), the actual maximum hold time should be supported by experimental studies (such as a challenge test). Microbiological samples must not be frozen, which would cause loss of viability.

questions.question: An incubator has a brief excursion below the temperature specified in the procedure (about 1°-2°). What example of handling does ⟨1117⟩ give?

options.A: Always treat it as invalid, resample all samples, and take the incubator out of service immediately until requalification is complete
options.B: No evaluation is needed because temperature excursions do not affect recovery; simply note the excursion in the incubator record
options.C: First evaluate the effect on recovery and document the investigation and disposition; for a brief, small low excursion, extending the incubation time may compensate
options.D: Immediately raise the incubator temperature by 5° to make up the lost time, then return to the specified incubation temperature

questions.explanation: The text requires evaluating the potential effect of a temperature excursion on samples and their disposition, and documenting the investigation and sample disposition. For example, a brief low excursion of about 1°-2° may be compensated by extending the incubation time; higher temperature excursions (for example above 40° for total aerobic count, or above 30° for yeast and mold count) require consideration of negative effects on recovery.

questions.question: Personnel who perform sampling need to enter the live culture area. What special precautions does ⟨1117⟩ require?

options.A: No restriction, as long as the mask is changed after leaving the live culture area, with no need for dedicated protective clothing or handwashing
options.B: Gloves are sufficient, with no special handwashing on leaving; the protective clothing may be worn back into general office areas and clean areas
options.C: They must enter wearing clean area garments and, after leaving, return directly to work in the clean area with no extra disinfection or handwashing
options.D: Wear dedicated protective clothing that is not worn outside the laboratory, wear gloves, and wash and disinfect hands thoroughly on leaving

questions.explanation: The text states that personnel engaged in sampling should not enter or work in the live culture area unless special precautions are taken, including wearing dedicated protective clothing that is not worn outside the laboratory, wearing gloves, and washing and disinfecting hands thoroughly on leaving, to reduce the chance of accidentally contaminating tests.

questions.question: What does ⟨1117⟩ expect regarding the competence of microbiology laboratory supervisors and managers?

options.A: Competence in microbiology at least as high as the personnel they supervise, with a core educational background in microbiology or a related biological science
options.B: An analytical chemistry background is enough, since the analytical principles of chemistry and microbiology are the same and no additional microbiology training is needed
options.C: An engineering background and budget management skills are enough, with no microbiology competence or understanding of laboratory operations required
options.D: New supervisors need no training and can be taught microbiology by their subordinates, as long as their management experience is extensive

questions.explanation: The text requires staff, supervisors and managers to have a core educational background in microbiology or a related biological science, and expects the microbiology competence of supervisors and managers to be at least as high as those they supervise. The biological principles that microbiology deals with differ greatly from analytical chemistry and engineering disciplines, and crossing over from another field is often difficult.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1117⟩ Competencies and Training of Personnel

questions.question: Which of the following is specifically mentioned in ⟨1117⟩ regarding analyst qualification?

options.A: A single assessment at hiring is enough, with no ongoing training or periodic requalification unless a major deviation occurs, and no training records needed
options.B: Only personnel performing sterility tests need qualification; other microbiology analysts need no form of qualification
options.C: Experienced personnel combined with periodic training and qualification (including periodic vision checks), which also applies to personnel who visually inspect media fill units
options.D: Analyst qualification is based mainly on written tests, with no assessment of practical skills and no periodic requalification

questions.explanation: The text states that hiring experienced personnel, together with periodic training and qualification (including periodic vision checks), limits the variability caused by analyst handling and interpretation of results to an acceptable level and ensures understanding of and adherence to good documentation practices; the same applies to personnel who visually inspect media fill units.

questions.question: Which scenario is an example listed in ⟨1117⟩ where a microbiological risk assessment can be used?

options.A: A routine incubator calibration date is about to expire
options.B: A new lot of medium passes growth-promotion testing
options.C: An analyst completes annual SOP training
options.D: Bioburden counts are elevated but still within specification

questions.explanation: The text lists situations where a microbiological risk assessment can be used, including elevated bioburden counts (but still within specification), atypical colonies after enrichment on selective agar, exceeding alert/action levels, and identification of organisms of concern. The risk assessment should be written and approved by personnel with microbiology education and experience.

questions.question: When microbiological testing is outsourced to a contract laboratory, what does ⟨1117⟩ expect of its reports?

options.A: The report should include the complete analytical worksheets, because a CoA with only a results summary does not provide the information needed to verify the data
options.B: A signed CoA summary is enough, with no need to provide raw worksheets or other source records for verifying test results, and no need to specify this in the quality agreement
options.C: The report need only state pass or fail, with the details kept by the contract laboratory and requested from it when needed
options.D: The report need not be linked to a pre-contract GMP compliance check, as long as the contract laboratory holds a general business license

questions.explanation: The text requires the report from a contract laboratory to include the complete analytical worksheets for the analysis, because a CoA with a results summary does not provide all the information needed to verify the test data. In addition, before contracting, the manufacturer should confirm that the contract laboratory complies with current GMP regulations and investigate the reputation and quality control performance of new or unfamiliar laboratories.
questions.reference: USP ⟨1117⟩ Laboratory Resources › Oversight of Contract Laboratories

questions.question: When transferring a validated microbiological method to another laboratory, what approach does ⟨1117⟩ recommend to gain greater assurance?

options.A: Comparative testing of the same sample in both laboratories, with consistent results being enough, since the same sample best reflects the transfer
options.B: Method suitability verification, since microbial cells are not uniformly distributed in a sample and comparative testing of the same sample may not be meaningful
options.C: Simply give the receiving laboratory the SOP and medium lot numbers with no verification, leaving the receiving laboratory to judge whether it applies
options.D: Personnel from the originating laboratory go to the receiving laboratory to run all tests and sign off the results, with receiving personnel only observing

questions.explanation: The text states that the performance of a validated method may vary from laboratory to laboratory, and differences in media, reagents, equipment, procedures and personnel experience can all affect results; because microbial cells are not uniformly distributed in samples, comparative testing of the same sample may not be applicable, and performing a method suitability verification gives the receiving unit greater confidence that it can perform the test.
